text: The most significant new religious figure of the New Kingdom of Egypt was Aten, who served as a representation of the god Ra and became the center of exclusive worship. This figure was the focus of Akhenaten's reign, a period marked by a distinctive style of art known as the Amarna Period.

text: Johannes Gutenberg is often associated with printing the first book using movable type in Germany. He introduced the metal movable-type printing press in Europe around 1450, along with innovations in casting the type based on a matrix and hand mould. This technology utilized an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony, which remained standard for 550 years.
title: Movable type

text: Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith from Mainz in Germany, is credited as the pioneer who created a metal movable-type printing system in Europe. During the period between 1436 and 1450, he refined hardware and techniques for casting letters from matrices using a device called the hand mould. This key invention provided the first practical method for producing cheap copies of letter punches in the vast quantities required to print complete books, thereby establishing movable-type printing as a viable enterprise.
title: Movable type

text: When a cell cannot be regenerated, the body replaces it with stromal connective tissue to maintain tissue/organ function. Stromal cells are the cells that support the parenchymal cells in any organ. Fibroblasts, immune cells, pericytes, and inflammatory cells are the most common types of stromal cells.
title: Cell damage

text: Trigger points form only in muscles, appearing as local contractions within a small number of muscle fibers that can pull on tendons and ligaments, causing pain deep within joints where no muscles exist. According to the integrated hypothesis theory, these points arise from excessive acetylcholine release, resulting in sustained depolarization of muscle fibers and an abnormal biochemical composition characterized by elevated acetylcholine, noradrenaline, and serotonin alongside a lower pH. This condition compresses local blood supply, creating a crisis of energy that generates sensitizing substances which interact with nociceptive nerves to produce localized pain at the neuromuscular junction. Consequently, the presence of trigger points in muscles often leads to associated pain and weakness, patterns that follow specific nerve pathways and have been mapped to identify the causative factors.
title: Myofascial trigger point

text: In the inaugural 2007 ICC World Twenty20 held in South Africa, India emerged victorious by defeating Pakistan in the final match. This tournament, lasting from September 11 to 24, 2007, featured twelve teams, including the finalists Kenya and Scotland, alongside the ten Test-playing nations.

text: In the 2007 ICC World Twenty20, India won the toss and chose to bat on a traditionally batsman-friendly pitch at the Bullring. Umar Gul took the wickets of both Yuvraj Singh and Mahendra Singh Dhoni, leaving India with 157/5 in 20 overs; only Gautam Gambhir (75 from 54 balls) produced a notable innings. A 21-run over from Sreesanth swung the game towards Pakistan. However, Irfan Pathan (3–16) and Joginder Sharma (2–20) slowed the scoring dramatically. With Pakistan needing 54 from 24 balls, Misbah-ul-Haq hit 3 sixes off Harbhajan Singh in one over. Sreesanth was also dispatched for 2 sixes but took the wicket of Sohail Tanvir, as Pakistan went into the last over needing 13 runs to win, with only 1 wicket remaining. Joginder Sharma bowled a wide first ball, followed by a dot ball. Misbah followed by taking six off a full-toss; Pakistan needed just 6 runs to win from the last four balls. Misbah attempted to hit the next ball with a paddle-scoop over fine leg, but he only managed to sky the ball, and it was caught at short fine-leg by Sreesanth, leaving Pakistan all out for 152 runs. Irfan Pathan was awarded the Man of the Match for his spell, which included 3 wickets for 16 runs, including that of Man of the Series, Shahid Afridi.
title: 2007 ICC World Twenty20

text: The Soviet Union (Russian: Сове́тский Сою́з, tr. Sovetsky Soyuz, IPA: [sɐˈvʲɛt͡skʲɪj sɐˈjus]) was a socialist state in Eurasia that existed from 1922 to 1991. Nominally a union of multiple national Soviet republics, its government and economy were highly centralized. The country was a one-party state, governed by the Communist Party with Moscow as its capital in its largest republic, the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. The Russian nation had constitutionally equal status among the many nations of the union but exerted de facto dominance in various respects. Other major urban centres were Leningrad, Kiev, Minsk, Alma-Ata and Novosibirsk. The Soviet Union was one of the five recognized nuclear weapons states and possessed the largest stockpile of weapons of mass destruction. It was a founding permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, as well as a member of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) and the leading member of the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (CMEA) and the Warsaw Pact.
title: Soviet Union

text: The red wolf, also known as the Florida black wolf or Mississippi Valley wolf, is a canid native to the southeastern United States and is a federally listed endangered species. text: Escherichia coli, also known as E. coli, is a Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium belonging to the genus Escherichia and is commonly located in the lower intestines of warm-blooded animals. While most strains are harmless and serve as part of the normal gut flora by producing vitamin K2 and preventing pathogenic colonization, certain serotypes can cause food poisoning or lead to product recalls due to contamination. The bacterium is expelled into the environment through fecal matter, where it thrives rapidly for three days under aerobic conditions before its population declines.
title: Escherichia coli

text: As the leader of the Yishuv, David Ben-Gurion was the first person to sign the Israeli Declaration of Independence. The document was intended for all 37 members of Moetzet HaAm, yet twelve could not attend, including eleven trapped in besieged Jerusalem and one abroad. The remaining 25 present were called up in alphabetical order to sign, with spaces reserved for those absent. Although a gap existed between the signatures of Eliyahu Dobkin and Meir Vilner, Zerach Warhaftig signed at the top of the following column, leading to speculation that Vilner's name was left blank to isolate him or to emphasize that even a communist had approved the declaration. Warhaftig later clarified that the space was left for him because, as a signatory trapped in Jerusalem, his Hebraised name would have fit alphabetically there; however, he insisted on signing under his actual name to honor his father's memory and therefore moved down two spaces. He and Vilner were the last surviving signatories, remaining close for the rest of their lives. Among the total signatories, two were women: Golda Meir and Rachel Cohen-Kagan.
title: Israeli Declaration of Independence

text: In the digestive systems of many organisms, chymotrypsin functions as a serine protease that catalyzes the hydrolysis of peptide bonds. While chymotrypsin naturally acts within living organisms, it can also hydrolyze amide bonds in a laboratory setting.

text: Christmas, though a Christian holiday, began as a celebration of the winter solstice. Many popular customs associated with Christmas developed independently of the commemoration of Jesus' birth, with certain elements having origins in pre-Christian festivals that were celebrated around the winter solstice by pagan populations who were later converted to Christianity. These elements, including the Yule log from Yule and gift giving from Saturnalia, became syncretized into Christmas over the centuries. The prevailing atmosphere of Christmas has also continually evolved since the holiday's inception, ranging from a sometimes raucous, drunken, carnival-like state in the Middle Ages, to a tamer family-oriented and children-centered theme introduced in a 19th-century transformation. In fact, the celebration of Christmas was banned on more than one occasion within certain Protestant groups, such as the Puritans, due to concerns that it was too pagan or unbiblical. Jehovah's Witnesses also reject the celebration of Christmas.
title: Christmas

text: The Beer Hall Putsch, also known as the Munich Putsch, and in German as the Hitlerputsch, was a failed coup attempt by Nazi Party leader Adolf Hitler, along with Generalquartiermeister Erich Ludendorff and other Kampfbund leaders, to seize power in Munich, Bavaria, during 8–9 November 1923. About two thousand Nazis marched to the centre of Munich, where they confronted the police, resulting in the death of 16 Nazis and four police officers. Although Hitler was not wounded during the clash, he locked his left arm with the right arm of Max Erwin von Scheubner-Richter, who was shot and killed, and was pulled to the pavement with him. Hitler escaped immediate arrest and was spirited off to safety in the countryside. After two days, Hitler was arrested and charged with treason.
title: Beer Hall Putsch

text: Christopher Columbus embarked on his first voyage from Spain in 1492, sailing with three ships including the Niña, Pinta, and Santa Maria to find a direct route to Asia. On October 12, 1492, he arrived at an island in the Bahamas, which he claimed for Spain, an event long viewed by Europeans as the discovery of America. This island was known as Guanahani to the Lucayans and San Salvador to the Spanish. While the identity of the first American landfall remains debated, many scholars accept Samuel E. Morison's identification of Columbus' San Salvador as what was later called Watling Island, a name officially renamed to San Salvador. Columbus visited several other islands in the Bahamas before proceeding to present-day Cuba and subsequently to Hispaniola.
title: History of the Bahamas

A mile and a half upstream from the city, 1,000 butchers gutted more than 300,000 animals per year. Animal entrails, known as offal, dung, blood, and urine contaminated New Orleans's drinking water, which was implicated in cholera outbreaks among the population.

text: By the late 1960s, various distinct rock music subgenres had emerged, including hybrids like blues rock, folk rock, country rock, raga rock, and jazz-rock, many of which contributed to the development of psychedelic rock. This genre was influenced by the countercultural psychedelic and hippie scene. In the second half of the 1970s, punk rock reacted by producing stripped-down, energetic social and political critiques. Punk was an influence in the 1980s on new wave, post-punk, and eventually alternative rock, which became a dominant force in rock music from the 1990s onward. From the 1990s, alternative rock began to break into the mainstream in the form of grunge, Britpop, and indie rock. Further fusion subgenres have since emerged, including pop punk, electronic rock, rap rock, and rap metal, as well as conscious attempts to revisit rock's history, including the garage rock/post-punk and synth-pop revivals at the beginning of the 2000s.
title: Rock music

text: The dynasty of the Qing originated in Manchuria, a region where the Jurchen Aisin Gioro clan established its presence. While the late sixteenth-century leader Nurhaci was initially a Ming vassal, he organized military-social units that incorporated elements from Jurchen, Han Chinese, and Mongol backgrounds. By 1636, his son Hong Taiji successfully expelled Ming forces from Liaodong and proclaimed the founding of the Qing. The dynasty's early rulers maintained their Manchu traditions, governing with a bureaucratic style that retained imperial examinations to recruit Han Chinese officials alongside Manchus. Although they adopted the title Emperor, they addressed Mongols as Bogd khaan and served as patrons of Tibetan Buddhism, while also adapting the tributary system to manage neighboring territories.
title: Qing dynasty

text: A subdural hematoma (SDH) is a type of hematoma that typically occurs following traumatic brain injury, where blood accumulates between the inner layer of the dura mater and the arachnoid mater. This condition arises most frequently due to tears in bridging veins that cross the subdural space, and these hemorrhages can lead to elevated intracranial pressure, potentially causing compression and damage to delicate brain tissue. While acute subdural hematomas are often life-threatening, chronic subdural hematomas may have a better prognosis if they are properly managed.
title: Subdural hematoma

text: The Chinese character for the umbrella, 傘 (sǎn), depicts a design that looks like a modern umbrella. While some theories suggest it started from large leaves tied to bough-like ribs or evolved from a tent, the prevailing tradition holds that it originated from standards and banners waving in the air. Consequently, the umbrella's use was frequently associated with high-ranking officials in China. On at least one occasion, twenty-four umbrellas were carried before the Emperor during a hunt, serving as a defense against rain rather than the sun. This design later traveled to Japan via Korea, Persia, and the Western world through the Silk Road, and the traditional Chinese and Japanese parasols near temples remain similar to the original ancient style.
title: Umbrella

text: In U.S. politics, general elections are elections held at various levels, such as city, county, congressional district, or state, that involve competition between at least two parties. text: The most common form of megalithic architecture in Europe is the portal tomb, a chamber consisting of upright stones (orthostats) with one or more large flat capstones forming a roof. Many of these structures, though by no means all, contain human remains, but it is debatable whether use as burial sites was their primary function. The megalithic structures of Malta are believed to be the oldest in Europe, in particular Skorba Temples. Though generally known as dolmens, the correct term accepted by archaeologists is portal tomb. However many local names exist, such as anta in Galicia and Portugal, stazzone in Sardinia, hunebed in the Netherlands, Hünengrab in Germany, dysse in Denmark, and cromlech in Wales. It is assumed that most portal tombs were originally covered by earthen mounds.

At the inn, Robin meets a man whose face looks like the devil, featuring two protrusions from his forehead and eyes burning like fire in a cave, who appears to be involved in many evil things. Later, Robin runs into this man again, but this time his face is painted black and red. After blocking his path with a cudgel, Robin finally gets the answer that his kinsman will soon pass by. He waits at the spot on the steps of a church where he is greeted by the first polite gentleman he has met all night. Soon, the two men hear the roar of an approaching mob. At its head is the man with the red and black face, and in its midst is Major Molineux, tarred and feathered. The crowd is in an uproar, and everyone is laughing. Soon, so is young Robin, as his eyes meet those of the Major, who knows him right away. Disillusioned, the youth asks the gentleman the way back to the ferry. text: The Canadian Pacific Railway began construction between 1881 and 1885, a timeframe that connects with earlier lines in the Ottawa Valley and Georgian Bay areas. The line served as Canada's first transcontinental railway, though it does not extend to the Atlantic coast. Primarily a freight railway, the CPR was for decades the sole practical method for long-distance passenger travel in most of Canada, playing a crucial role in the settlement and development of Western regions. The corporation grew into one of Canada's largest and most powerful entities, holding that status until 1975. Passenger services were discontinued in 1986, following the company's acquisition by Via Rail Canada in 1978. In 1885, a beaver was selected as the railway's logo to honor Sir Donald A Smith, who had risen from factor to governor of the Hudson's Bay Company. Smith financed the project with much of his personal wealth, and he personally drove the final spike to complete the transcontinental line.
title: Canadian Pacific Railway

text: The vascular cambium is a plant tissue located between the xylem and the phloem in the stems and roots of certain vascular plants. It is the source of both secondary xylem growth inwards towards the pith, and secondary phloem growth outwards to the bark. text: Wealth inequality in the United States is a persistent and widening gap where the top 1% controls a disproportionately large share of the nation's resources. Just prior to President Obama's 2014 State of the Union Address, media reports indicated that the wealthiest 1% possess 40% of the nation's wealth, while the bottom 80% own only 7%. This disparity has continued to grow, with the richest 1 percent in the United States now owning more additional income than the bottom 90 percent. The gap between the top 10% and the middle class is already over 1,000%, and that increases another 1,000% for the top 1%. The average employee needs to work more than a month to earn what the CEO earns in one hour. Although different from income inequality, the two are related. In Inequality for All—a 2013 documentary with Robert Reich in which he argued that income inequality is the defining issue for the United States—Reich states that 95% of economic gains went to the top 1% net worth (HNWI) since 2009 when the recovery allegedly started. More recently, in 2017, an Oxfam study found that eight rich people, six of them Americans, own as much combined wealth as half the human race.
title: Wealth inequality in the United States

text: In 2007, the top 1% of the American population held 35% of the nation's total wealth, while the next 19% owned 51%. Later data from 2011 showed that financial inequality had increased further, as the top 1% owned 43% of the wealth, the next 19% owned 50%, and the bottom 80% owned just 7%. Despite the rise in overall inequality, the top 1% still controls a large portion of the wealth, though their share grew slightly from 35% to 37% following the Great Recession, which began in 2007.

text: Iron ore deposits were known in Australia, with the Mount Whaleback deposit discovered in 1957 by Stan Hilditch. However, mining did not begin in earnest until 1960, when the Australian Government lifted an embargo on iron ore exports due to concerns about the mineral's short supply. text: Havana Harbor served as the site where the U.S. ship Maine was lost on the evening of February 15, 1898. Although a subsequent inquiry into the sinking's cause and responsibility became unclear, public sentiment in the United States, fueled by sensationalist articles from the "yellow press," largely blamed Spain. This sentiment fueled the rallying cry "Remember the Maine! To hell with Spain!", which became a driving force behind the subsequent Spanish-American War. While the sinking was not the direct cause of war, it acted as a catalyst, hastening the diplomatic impasse between the two nations.

text: The National Football League Draft is an event where each team has its representatives attend to select players. In round 7, and for compensatory picks, teams only have 4 minutes to make their choice. If a team does not make a decision within its allotted time, the team still can submit its selection at any time after its time is up, but the next team can pick before it, thus possibly 'stealing' a player the team with the earlier pick may have been considering. This occurred in the 2003 draft, when the Minnesota Vikings, with the 7th overall pick, were late with their selection. The Jacksonville Jaguars drafted quarterback Byron Leftwich and the Carolina Panthers drafted offensive tackle Jordan Gross before the Vikings were able to submit their selection of defensive tackle Kevin Williams. This also happened in 2011; as the Baltimore Ravens were negotiating a trade with the Chicago Bears, their time expired and allowed the Kansas City Chiefs to pick ahead of Baltimore, who was unable to finalize the trade with Chicago.

text: Wave–particle duality describes how electromagnetic radiation propagates as linear waves while simultaneously acting as discrete particles, a concept that was crucial for explaining the photoelectric effect. If one assumes that light energy is transferred in integer multiples of Planck's constant times its frequency, low-frequency light fails to eject high-energy electrons because each individual photon carries insufficient energy. Only by increasing the frequency of the light—thereby raising the energy of each photon—can electrons be ejected with higher energy. This relationship, where the energy of ejected electrons increases linearly with frequency, was confirmed by Robert Andrews Millikan in 1915, who found experimental results in perfect accord with Einstein's predictions. Although the energy of ejected electrons reflected Planck's constant, the explicit proof of the photon's existence as a discrete particle came later with the discovery of the photon antibunching effect. When Einstein received his Nobel Prize in 1921, it was not awarded for his special and general relativity, but for his simple yet revolutionary suggestion of quantized light. Einstein's "light quanta" would not be called photons until 1925, but even in 1905 they represented the quintessential example of wave-particle duality, as electromagnetic radiation can only be emitted or absorbed as discrete elements.
title: Wave–particle duality

text:
# pH
In chemistry, pH (potential of hydrogen) is a numeric scale used to specify the acidity or basicity of an aqueous solution. It is approximately the negative of the base 10 logarithm of the activity of the hydrogen ion, measured in units of moles per liter, of hydrogen ions. More precisely it is the negative of the base 10 logarithm of the activity of the hydrogen ion. Solutions with a pH less than 7 are acidic and solutions with a pH greater than 7 are basic. Pure water is neutral, at pH 7 (25 °C), being neither an acid nor a base. Contrary to popular belief, the pH value can be less than 0 or greater than 14 for very strong acids and bases respectively.
title: pH

text: Sunflowers (original title, in French: Tournesols) refers to two distinct series of still life paintings created by the Dutch artist Vincent van Gogh. The initial set was painted in Paris in 1887, featuring flowers resting on the ground, whereas the second collection was executed a year later in Arles and displays a bouquet of sunflowers arranged in a vase. In the artist's perspective, these two versions were connected through the name of his friend Paul Gauguin, who owned two of the Parisian pieces. Approximately eight months after the first work, van Gogh intended to impress Gauguin further by including Sunflowers within the painted Décoration for the Yellow House, which served as the guestroom for his residence in Arles. text: Surface area is a critical factor in biological function because the total amount of surface available determines the efficiency of a process. In the context of gas exchange, this principle is essential for organisms to obtain and release gases. Small organisms, such as bacteria and protozoa, possess a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, meaning their gas exchange membrane is typically just the cell membrane itself. Larger organisms, which have a small surface-area-to-volume ratio, rely on specialized structures with convoluted surfaces to create a large area for effective gas exchange. Examples of these specialized structures include gills found in molluscs, pulmonary alveoli in mammals, and spongy mesophyll inside plant leaves. These convoluted surfaces may sometimes be internalized into the body of the organism, such as the inner surface of the mammalian lung or the spongy mesophyll found in plant leaves.
title: Gas exchange

text: Sedimentary rock is the dominant rock type found on the Earth's surface, covering approximately 73% of the current land area. These rocks are deposited in layers as strata, creating a structure known as bedding. The study of these formations provides valuable information for civil engineering projects such as road construction and tunnel building. Additionally, sedimentary rocks serve as important sources of natural resources, including coal, fossil fuels, drinking water, and ores.
title: Sedimentary rock

text: Taylor is a surname used in the British Isles that traces its roots to French and Latin, originating as a Norman occupational name for a tailor in France. text: Sport psychology sub-fields of performance enhancement focus on the management of arousal to optimize outcomes. Arousal regulation involves entering and maintaining an optimal level of cognitive and physiological activation, which may include relaxation techniques like progressive muscle relaxation, breathing exercises, or meditation to reduce anxiety, or energizing cues such as listening to music to increase alertness. The Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment (MAC) Theory, a primary form of mindfulness in sport, was developed in 2001 with the goal of maximizing human potential for a meaningful life. This theory employs specific meditation and acceptance protocols tested on athletes like NCAA basketball player Frank L. Gardner, who saw her personal satisfaction in her performances rise from 2.4 to 9.2 out of 10 after several weeks of the protocol. Additionally, the effect of mental barriers on her game decreased from 8 out of 8 to 2.2 out of 8 during the same period. Research by Gardner and Zella Moore further demonstrated that when the MAC protocol is tailored to a specific population, such as an adolescent competitive diver, it can provide performance enhancement, resulting in a 13 to 14 percent increase in diving scores after the protocol was implemented.
title: Sport psychology

text: The term "cradle of civilization" refers to locations where, according to current archaeological data, civilization is understood to have emerged. While there was no single "cradle," several distinct civilizations developed independently, with the Fertile Crescent (Mesopotamia and Ancient Egypt) recognized as the earliest. Other notable origins include the Indo-Gangetic Plain in the Indian subcontinent and the Yellow River in China. Scholars also note that the civilizations of Mesoamerica and Norte Chico in present-day Peru emerged independently from those in Eurasia.
title: Cradle of civilization

text:
Cradle of civilization

Around 10,200 BC, the first fully developed Neolithic cultures emerged in the fertile crescent, a region that subsequently spread east and west. Among the most significant of these early settlements is Jericho in the Levant, which is believed to be the world's first town, established around 8500 BC and fortified by 6800 BC. In Mesopotamia, the convergence of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers created rich soil and reliable water sources essential for irrigation. The civilizations that rose from these river valleys represent the earliest known non-nomadic agrarian societies. Consequently, the fertile crescent and Mesopotamia are frequently cited as the cradle of civilization.

The Ubaid period, spanning from approximately 6500 to 3800 BC, marks the earliest known era on the alluvial plain, though earlier phases may have been obscured by sediment. During this time, urbanization began, as agriculture and animal husbandry became widespread in sedentary communities, especially in Northern Mesopotamia. Intensive irrigated hydraulic agriculture also commenced in the southern regions. Eridu, the oldest Sumerian site, was settled around 5300 BC, while the city of Ur first appeared at the conclusion of this period. The Ubaid era lasted for several millennia, eventually giving way to the Uruk period.
title: Cradle of civilization

text: The term "anatomy" is commonly taken to refer to human anatomy, though substantially the same structures and tissues are found throughout the rest of the animal kingdom, and the term also includes the anatomy of other animals. text: Anatomy, along with physiology and biochemistry, constitutes a fundamental branch of science focused on the structure of human body parts. This field is typically introduced to medical students during their initial year at medical school, where it may be explored either regionally or systematically. While regional studies examine areas like the head and chest, systematic approaches investigate specific systems such as the nervous or respiratory structures. A prominent example of major anatomy literature is Gray's Anatomy, which has shifted from a systems-based format to a regional layout to align with contemporary pedagogical standards. Consequently, a comprehensive understanding of anatomy is essential for physicians, particularly surgeons and specialists in diagnostic fields like histopathology and radiology.
title: Anatomy

text: The woolly mammoth was roughly the same size as modern African elephants, with males reaching shoulder heights between 2.7 and 3.4 meters and females reaching 2.6–2.9 meters. While newborn calves weighed about 90 kilograms, individuals could probably reach the age of 60. The diet of the woolly mammoth was mainly grass and sedges. Its habitat was the mammoth steppe, which stretched across northern Eurasia and North America. The animal was well adapted to the cold environment during the last ice age, covered in fur with an outer covering of long guard hairs and a shorter undercoat. Its ears and tail were short to minimize frostbite and heat loss, and it had long, curved tusks and four molars, which were replaced six times during the lifetime of an individual.
title: Woolly mammoth

text: Woolly mammoths sustained themselves on plant food, mainly grass and sedges, which were supplemented with herbaceous plants, flowering plants, shrubs, mosses, and tree matter. The composition and exact varieties differed from location to location. An adult of six tonnes would need to eat 180 kg (397 lb) daily, and may have foraged as long as twenty hours every day. The two-fingered tip of the trunk was probably adapted for picking up the short grasses of the last ice age (Quaternary glaciation, 2.58 million years ago to present) by wrapping around them, whereas modern elephants curl their trunks around the longer grass of their tropical environments. The trunk could also be used for pulling off large grass tufts, delicately picking buds and flowers, and tearing off leaves and branches where trees and shrubs were present. The "Yukagir mammoth" had ingested plant matter that contained spores of dung fungus.[54] Isotope analysis shows that woolly mammoths fed mainly on C3 plants, unlike horses and rhinos.[55]
title: Woolly mammoth

text: The process of mitosis is divided into stages corresponding to the completion of one set of activities and the start of the next. These stages are prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase. During mitosis, the chromosomes, which have already duplicated, condense and attach to spindle fibers that pull one copy of each chromosome to opposite sides of the cell. The result is two genetically identical daughter nuclei. The rest of the cell may then continue to divide by cytokinesis to produce two daughter cells. Producing three or more daughter cells instead of normal two is a mitotic error called tripolar mitosis or multipolar mitosis. Other errors during mitosis can induce apoptosis or cause mutations. Certain types of cancer can arise from such mutations.
title: Mitosis

text: While the PDCA model gained widespread popularity with W. Edwards Deming, who is often hailed as the father of modern quality control, Deming himself frequently referred to the original cycle as the "Shewhart cycle." It was later in his career that Deming modified the process to "Plan, Do, Study, Act," or PDSA, a change driven by his belief that the term "check" implied mere inspection rather than analytical study. This PDSA cycle was instrumental in developing the model of know-how transfer processes and other related frameworks.
title: PDCA

text: Joseph Nye Welch, an American lawyer active from 1890 to 1960, served as the chief counsel for the U.S. Army during its investigation into Communist activities, a period known as the Army–McCarthy hearings. During this confrontation with Senator Joseph McCarthy, Welch famously posed the question, "At long last, have you left no sense of decency?" This moment is recognized as a pivotal turning point in the history of McCarthyism.
title: Joseph N. Welch

text: In 2000, the De Beers business model changed because of factors such as the decision by producers in Canada and Australia to distribute diamonds outside the De Beers channel, as well as rising awareness of blood diamonds that forced De Beers to "avoid the risk of bad publicity" by limiting sales to its own mined products. De Beers' market share of rough diamonds fell from as high as 90% in the 1980s to 33% in 2013, because of a more fragmented diamond market bringing greater competition, as well as more transparency and greater liquidity.
title: De Beers

text: After the birth of their child, Claire and Alex Ryan begin a relationship, with Alex planning to propose to her during a party. Claire, Tess, and baby Charlotte are returning from town with party supplies when their Ute hits a pothole and Claire loses control of the vehicle, coming to a stop with its front wheels dangling off the edge of a cliff. Tess is able to get out and get Charlotte to safety, but cannot get Claire's door open before the Ute starts to slide. It goes over the cliff and into a canyon, killing Claire.

text: While Tarapur is the largest nuclear power station in India, the specific facility located in Narora, Kakrapar, Tarapur is known as the Atomic Power Station. This site was constructed with two boiling water reactor (BWR) units by Bechtel and GE under the 1963 123 Agreement between India, the United States, and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). These units were brought online for commercial operation on 28 October 1969 with an initial power of 210 MW of electricity, which was later reduced to 160 MW due to technical difficulties. These were the first of their kind in Asia, marking a significant milestone in nuclear energy development.
title: Tarapur Atomic Power Station

The song, performed by the members Marie Fredriksson and Per Gessle, reached the top of the US Hot 100 chart and secured four number-one spots on the Billboard Hot 100. These chart-topping achievements, alongside their previous success, formed the foundation of the group's international career, which also saw the release of the breakthrough album Look Sharp! in the late 1980s.
title: Roxette

text: The tibia and fibula bones are located in the leg. The fibula is a leg bone situated on the lateral side of the tibia, with which it is connected above and below. It is the smaller of the two bones, and, in proportion to its length, the slenderest of all the long bones. Its upper extremity is small, placed toward the back of the head of the tibia, below the level of the knee joint, and excluded from the formation of this joint. Its lower extremity inclines a little forward, so as to be on a plane anterior to that of the upper end; it projects below the tibia, and forms the lateral part of the ankle-joint.
title: Fibula

text: The breakup of Yugoslavia occurred after the Allied victory in World War II, when the country was established as a federation of six republics: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Slovenia. Two autonomous provinces were also created within Serbia, including Vojvodina and Kosovo. Each republic maintained its own branch of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia party and a ruling elite, with tensions resolved at the federal level. The Yugoslav model of state organization, along with a "middle way" between planned and liberal economy, had been a relative success, allowing for strong economic growth and political stability up to the 1980s under the rule of president-for-life Josip Broz Tito. Following his death in 1980, the weakened federal system was left unable to cope with rising economic and political challenges.
title: Breakup of Yugoslavia

text: The won (/wʌn/; Korean: 원, Korean pronunciation: [wʌn]; symbol: ₩; code: KRW) is the official currency of South Korea. A single won is divided into 100 jeon, the monetary subunit, which is no longer used for everyday transactions. The won is issued by the Bank of Korea, based in the capital city of Seoul.
title: South Korean won

text: Molecular clouds in interstellar space serve as the primary locations where star formation occurs today, functioning as dense regions that collapse to form stars. These areas are often described as stellar nurseries or star-forming regions, and they are essential precursors to the star formation process. The study of these giant molecular clouds and protostars as immediate products is a key branch of astronomy, closely related to planet formation.
title: Star formation

text: While Karnataka officially became part of India on August 15, 1947, a distinct historical reality existed in certain regions under the Nizam's rule in Hyderabad. These areas, comprising parts of the former Bidar, Gulbarga, and Raichur districts, were not immediately integrated. The Lingayat minority in these regions, having long resented Nizam governance and Razakar oppression, demanded freedom. Consequently, the Nizam refused to cede power until his regime was overthrown by force. Following this military intervention, Hyderabad province and its inhabitants declared independence on September 17, 1948. This date is now commemorated by the Karnataka government as the official Hyderabad-Karnataka liberation day.
title: Unification of Karnataka

The king had previously invited Giovanni da Verrazzano to explore the eastern coast of North America on behalf of France in 1524. Le Veneur cited voyages to Newfoundland and Brazil as proof of Cartier's ability to "lead ships to the discovery of new lands in the New World."

text: The Canterbury Tales, a collection of 24 stories written by Geoffrey Chaucer between 1387 and 1400, revolves around a pilgrimage undertaken by a group of pilgrims. Their primary goal is to visit the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral, and the entire expedition serves as the backdrop for a storytelling contest held by the group.

text: Mark Sloan first appears in season two as a highly respected otolaryngologist sub-specialized in plastic surgery, the childhood best friend of neurosurgeon Derek Shepherd. In his debut, he flirts with Meredith Grey, an encounter that ends with Derek punching him in the face. Later, it is revealed that Mark had an affair with his wife, Addison, while they were living in New York. Mark travels to Seattle, intent on convincing Addison to return with him, but his offer is rejected and Derek declines to renew their friendship. Mark returns during season three at Addison's drunken behest, but she again rejects him once sober. Undeterred, Mark sells his successful private practice and takes over the plastics program at Seattle Grace Hospital. During Meredith's morphine rampage, Mark finds out about his nickname McSteamy which was given to him by her during his first trip to Seattle back when he attempted to get Addison back and earn Derek's friendship back. It is later revealed that Mark has at some point slept with all of Derek's sisters. Mark has a brief fling with Addison's friend, orthopedic surgeon Callie Torres, and develops a friendship with Derek's girlfriend, intern Meredith Grey. It is revealed that after Derek left New York, Mark and Addison continued their relationship for two months, during which she conceived and aborted his child. Just weeks after moving to Seattle he quickly observes that Derek's true love was Meredith and tries to convince Addison that her marriage with Derek was over. Mark enters into a sixty-day abstinence pact with Addison, agreeing that if they can remain celibate for that time, Addison will give their relationship another chance. Addison ultimately breaks the pact by having sex with intern Alex Karev, and soon thereafter departs from Seattle to work in Los Angeles.

text: The most recent technological change to the U.S. economy is the digitization of social systems, which marks the fifth Kondratiev wave of technological change. This shift, occurring from 1940 to 1970, was characterized by motorization and the automated mobilization of society, with the most recent iteration being the digitization of social systems. According to Carlota Perez, this digital transformation fulfills the conditions of a general purpose technology by providing a key factor with clearly perceived low-and descending-relative cost, unlimited supply, and the potential for all-pervasiveness. Consequently, digital Information and Communication Technologies represent a general purpose technology that can transform an entire economy, leading to a modern, developed form of socio-economic and political organization often referred to as the post-industrial society, the information society, or the digital age.
title: Digital Revolution

text: Both ethnic affiliation and membership in specific biraderis or zaat/quoms serve as additional integral components of social identity. Within the bounds of endogamy defined by these parameters, close consanguineous unions are preferred due to the congruence of key features of group- and individual-level background factors. McKim Marriott claims that a social stratification which is hierarchical, closed, endogamous, and hereditary is widely prevalent, particularly in the western parts of Pakistan. Frederik Barth, however, in his review of this system of social stratification in Pakistan, suggested that these characteristics constitute castes.
title: Caste

text: The Battle of Issus took place in southern Anatolia on November 5, 333 BC, during the second major conflict of Alexander the Great's conquest of Asia. This confrontation occurred between the Hellenic League, led by Alexander, and the Achaemenid Empire, commanded by Darius III, following the earlier Battle of the Granicus where the Persian satraps of Asia Minor had been defeated by Greek mercenaries. Darius subsequently gathered reinforcements and led his forces in a surprise march behind the Macedonian advance to sever their supply lines. This strategic maneuver forced Alexander to counter-march, positioning the two armies near the mouth of the Pinarus River and the town of Issus for the decisive engagement.
title: Battle of Issus

This period was characterized by high unemployment, poverty, low profits, deflation, and a sudden loss of confidence in the economic future.
title: Great Depression in the United States

text: Aegisthus was the son of Thyestes and Pelopia, who had been the children of Atreus and his twin brother. After discovering Thyestes' adultery with his wife Aerope, Atreus killed their children and fed them to Thyestes. Aegisthus subsequently vowed gruesome revenge on Atreus' children. Aegisthus successfully murdered Atreus and restored his father to the throne, taking possession of the throne of Mycenae and jointly ruling with Thyestes. During this period, Agamemnon and his brother Menelaus took refuge with Tyndareus, King of Sparta, and respectively married Tyndareus' daughters Clytemnestra and Helen. Agamemnon and Clytemnestra had four children: one son, Orestes, and three daughters, Iphigenia, Electra, and Chrysothemis. Menelaus succeeded Tyndareus in Sparta, while Agamemnon, with his brother's assistance, drove out Aegisthus and Thyestes to recover his father's kingdom. He extended his dominion by conquest and became the most powerful prince in Greece.
title: Agamemnon

text: J. Wellington Wimpy is a fictional character known for his all-time favorite food, hamburgers, who is frequently depicted carrying or eating one or more burgers at a time. A recurring joke involves his attempts to con patrons into buying his meal for him, starting with the catchphrase from 1931: "Cook me up a hamburger. I'll pay you Thursday." This evolved in 1932 into the famous line, "I'll gladly pay you Tuesday for a hamburger today." The phrase was also slightly altered in the episode "Spree Lunch" to "I'll have a hamburger, for which I will gladly pay you Tuesday." This expression is now commonly used to illustrate financial irresponsibility and still appears in modern comedies such as The Drew Carey Show and The Office. The initial part of the phrase was even the title of Episode 6 of the fourth season of Cheers, "I'll Gladly Pay You Tuesday."
title: J. Wellington Wimpy

text: Tug-of-war has been a team event at the Summer Olympics since 1900, making 1920 the most recent year before the sport was discontinued. The first instance of a country winning all three medals occurred in 1904 by the United States, while the first podium finish was achieved by British teams in 1908.
title: Tug of war at the Summer Olympics

text: The term "Rightly Guided Caliphs" describes the 30-year reign of the first four successors following the death of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, collectively known as "the Rashidun." While the specific concept of "Rightly Guided Caliphs" is historically linked to the later Abbasid Caliphate, in Sunni Islam it refers to the 30-year reign of the first four caliphs (successors) Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman ibn Affan, and Ali of the Rashidun Caliphate, the first caliphate. This designation is derived from the Sunni imperative "Hold firmly to my example (sunnah) and that of the Rightly Guided Caliphs" (Ibn Majah, Abu Dawood).[1]
title: Rashidun

text: Itai-itai disease was a form of poisoning caused by cadmium released in significant quantities by mining operations, which began in 1910 and continued through 1945. This pollution originated from the Kamioka Mines in Toyama Prefecture, where cadmium was used to produce gold, silver, lead, copper, and zinc. The disease first appeared around 1912, shortly after cadmium emissions started, and persisted until the end of World War II. Prior to the war, the Mitsui Mining & Smelting Co., Ltd. increased mining operations to satisfy wartime demand, leading to severe contamination of the Jinzū River and its tributaries, which were essential for irrigation, drinking water, and other downstream uses.
title: Itai-itai disease

text: The Confederate States of America was a political entity that emerged from the desire of many southern whites to maintain independence from the larger United States, a sentiment they termed Southern nationalism or the "Cause." This regionalism transcended simple states' rights and deeply intertwined with cultural and financial dependence on the South's slavery-based economy. Consequently, the Confederacy's policies were driven by a convergence of race, slavery, politics, and economics, raising almost all South-related issues to the status of moral questions rather than mere ways of life. The war that tested the Confederacy's existence was not merely a conflict over territory but a struggle where national political parties, national churches, and interstate families divided along sectional lines. Historians note that the leaders of the secession movement explicitly cited the defense of slavery as their prime motive, acknowledging that recognizing the centrality of slavery to the Confederacy is essential for understanding its nature.
title: Confederate States of America

text: The urinary bladder is situated below the peritoneal cavity near the pelvic floor and behind the pubic symphysis. In men, it lies in front of the rectum, separated by the recto-vesical pouch, and is supported by fibres of the levator ani and of the prostate gland. In women, it lies in front of the uterus, separated by the vesico-uterine pouch, and is supported by the elevator ani and the upper part of the vagina. The wall of the urinary bladder is normally 3–5 mm thick.
title: Urinary bladder

text: Ideology is defined as a coherent set of values and beliefs about public policy. This concept represents a system of ideas that relies on a few basic assumptions about reality, which may or may not have any factual basis. Ideas become ideologies through the subjective ongoing choices people make, serving as the seed around which further thought grows. According to most recent analysis, ideologies are neither necessarily right nor wrong; rather, believers in ideology range from passive acceptance through fervent advocacy to true belief. An excessive need for certitude lurks at fundamentalist levels in politics and religions.
title: Ideology

text: In social studies, a political ideology is defined as a coherent set of values and beliefs concerning public policy. This ethical set of ideals, principles, doctrines, myths, or symbols originates from a social movement, institution, class, or large group. Such ideologies explain how society should function and provide a political and cultural blueprint for a specific social order. They are concerned with diverse societal aspects, including the economy, education, health care, labor law, criminal law, the justice system, social security, trade, the environment, minors, immigration, race, the military, patriotism, and established religion.
title: Ideology

text: A large-scale example of an action performed by the cytoskeleton is muscle contraction. In the muscle, there are groups of highly specialized cells that work together to perform this function. A main component in the cytoskeleton that helps show the true function of this muscle contraction is a microfilament. Microfilaments are composed of the most abundant cellular protein known as actin. During contraction of a muscle, within each muscle cell, myosin molecular motors collectively exert forces on parallel actin filaments. Muscle contraction starts from nerve impulses which then causes increased amounts of calcium to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Increases in calcium in the cytosol allow muscle contraction to begin with the help of two proteins, tropomyosin and troponin. Tropomyosin inhibits the interaction between actin and myosin, while troponin senses the increase in calcium and releases the inhibition. This action contracts the muscle cell, and through the synchronous process in many muscle cells, the entire muscle.
title: Cytoskeleton

text: Glycogen functions as a glucose polymer, serving as a primary energy storage molecule in plants. text: The ulnar nerve is a nerve that runs near the ulna bone, where it is in relation with the ulnar collateral ligament of the elbow joint. This nerve is the largest unprotected nerve in the human body, meaning it is not protected by muscle or bone, so injury is common. It is directly connected to the little finger and the adjacent half of the ring finger, innervating the palmar aspect of these fingers, including both front and back of the tips, perhaps as far back as the fingernail beds.
title: Ulnar nerve

text: This nerve can cause an electric shock-like sensation by striking the medial epicondyle of the humerus from posteriorly, or inferiorly with the elbow flexed. This name is thought to be a pun, based on the sound resemblance between the name of the bone of the upper arm, the "humerus" and the word "humorous." Alternatively, according to the Oxford English Dictionary it may refer to "the peculiar sensation experienced when it is struck."

text: Neuropsychology is the experimental study of how brain functioning influences behavior and cognition, aiming to understand the link between the mind and neurological disorders. While classical neurology focuses on the physiology of the nervous system and classical psychology is largely divorced from it, neuropsychology seeks to discover how the brain correlates with the mind. It is an experimental field concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of behavioral and cognitive effects resulting from neurological conditions, making use of neuroscience and an information processing view of the mind similar to cognitive psychology and science. This field has been applied to lesion studies in humans and animals, as well as to efforts to record electrical activity from individual cells in higher primates.
title: Neuropsychology

text: Experimental neuropsychology is an approach that utilizes methods from experimental psychology to uncover how the nervous system and cognitive function interact. While most of this field involves studying healthy humans in a laboratory setting, a small number of researchers conduct animal experiments. The discipline often leverages specific features of our nervous system, such as the fact that visual information presented to a specific visual field is preferentially processed by the cortical hemisphere on the opposite side, to establish connections between neuroanatomy and psychological function.
title: Neuropsychology

text: The first element on the periodic table is hydrogen, which corresponds to atomic number 1. This element is the lightest and most abundant of all known chemical substances, and its discovery predates the systematic naming of the rest of the table. The periodic table currently displays the first seven rows of elements, with hydrogen occupying the top-left corner of the first period. While many elements exist naturally, the first 94 elements are found in nature, though some are rare and were first synthesized in laboratories before being discovered in their natural forms. Elements with atomic numbers from 95 to 118 have only been created in laboratories or nuclear reactors, and the most recent additions to the table, including oganesson, were officially named and confirmed by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry in 2016.
title: Periodic table

text: As of 2016, the periodic table lists 118 confirmed elements, beginning with Hydrogen at position 1 and concluding with Oganesson at position 118. While the most recent additions—elements 113, 115, 117, and 118—were officially recognized by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry in December 2015, their proposed names, nihonium, moscovium, tennessine, and oganesson, were formally announced by the IUPAC in June 2016 and adopted in November 2016.

text: Spinal fusion, also known as spondylodesis or spondylosyndesis, is a surgical technique that joins two or more vertebrae. The process typically involves using bone grafting—either from the patient, a donor, or artificial substitutes—to help the bones heal together, while additional hardware like screws, plates, or cages is often used to hold the bones in place during the healing process.
title: Spinal fusion

text: Sonnet 116, one of Shakespeare's most celebrated love sonnets, has faced scholarly debate regarding its true thematic interpretation. Hilton Landry suggests that viewing this poem as a pure celebration of genuine love is flawed, largely because its surrounding context within the sequence of adjacent sonnets has not been fully appreciated. While Landry admits the poem possesses a broad, almost universal quality, he cautions that its meaning is inherently limited to a specific range rather than being universally applicable. This limitation exists precisely because the poem does not function as an isolated work but rather as part of a distinct group of three sonnets—94, 116, and 129—that are separated from the rest of Shakespeare's output by a sense of detachment. In this trio, the subject matter of love is removed, creating a unique perspective on the nature of love and its experience that differs from the typical patterns found elsewhere in his work. Consequently, critics like Neely argue that one cannot rely on external context to determine the tone of this specific sonnet, as there is no authoritative sequence to serve as positive evidence for its emotional stance. Furthermore, since the poet does not seek to resolve the central issues of the poem, it follows that no definitive conclusion can be drawn from the text alone.
title: Sonnet 116

text: Advisory speed limits are traffic signs that provide information about hazards or conditions ahead, rather than enforcing a mandatory speed. In the United States, these signs typically appear as a small yellow sign placed under a main warning sign or as a standalone variation on the standard speed limit sign, featuring a yellow background instead of white. The words "speed limit" are omitted, and an additional panel specifies the type of hazard. Although these signs list specific speeds, they are classified as warning signs, not regulatory signs, because primary speed signs are regulatory. Australia uses a similar design, while Germany employs a square sign with a blue background and white lettering, similar to a minimum speed limit sign. New Zealand uses a yellow background with black lettering, resembling the Australian design but without "km/h" lettering. The United Kingdom currently uses an oblong white rectangle with black lettering stating "Max Speed."
title: Advisory speed limit

text: Medium of exchange is a standard unit or measure of wealth that satisfies specific criteria, such as being free floating and depending upon its supply market to find or set a value that continues to change as the supply of money is changed with respect to the economy's demand. Critics of the prevailing system of fiat money argue that fiat money is the root cause of the continuum of economic crises, since it leads to the dominance of fraud, corruption, and manipulation precisely because it does not satisfy the criteria for a medium of exchange cited above. Specifically, prevailing fiat money is free floating and depending upon its supply market finds or sets a value to it that continues to change as the supply of money is changed with respect to the economy's demand. Increasing free floating money supply with respect to needs of the economy reduces the quantity of the basket of the goods and services to which it is linked by the market and that provides it purchasing power. Thus it is not a unit or standard measure of wealth and its manipulation impedes the market mechanism by that it sets/determine just prices. That leads us to a situation where no value-related economic data is just or reliable. On the other hand, Chartalists claim that the ability to manipulate the value of fiat money is an advantage, in that fiscal stimulus is more easily available in times of economic crisis.
title: Medium of exchange

text: Serialism of the first type is most specifically defined as the structural principle according to which a recurring series of ordered elements (normally a set—or row—of pitches or pitch classes) are used in order or manipulated in particular ways to give a piece unity. This approach, often broadly applied to all music written in what Arnold Schoenberg called "The Method of Composing with Twelve Notes related only to one another" (Schoenberg 1975, 218; Anon. n.d.), or dodecaphony, and methods that evolved from his methods, is sometimes used more specifically to apply only to music where at least one element other than pitch is subjected to being treated as a row or series. In such usages post-Webernian serialism will be used to denote works that extend serial techniques to other elements of music, with other terms used to make the distinction being twelve-note serialism for the former, and integral serialism for the latter.
title: Serialism

text: Veronica is a female given name whose English meaning is derived from the Greek words "berenike," which translates to "she who brings victory." This name originated as a transliteration of the Greek name Berenice, representing the Macedonian form of the Athenian name Phereníkē. The etymology traces back to the verb *phérein* (to bring) and the noun *nίκη* (victory), thus defining the name as "she who brings victory." This meaning was solidified during the Hellenistic age when the name became popular among royal dynasties of the Diadochi, particularly the Ptolemies and Seleucids, who favored it as a feminine royal name. While medieval etymology sometimes erroneously linked the name to Latin *vera* (true), its enduring popularity stems primarily from the veneration of Saint Veronica and her associated veil in Christian tradition.
title: Veronica (name)

text: Kraków (Polish pronunciation: [ˈkrakuf]) is the second largest and one of the oldest cities in Poland, situated on the Vistula River in the Lesser Poland region. Situated on the Vistula River (Polish: Wisła) in the Lesser Poland (Polish: Małopolska) region, the city dates back to the 7th century. Kraków has traditionally been one of the leading centres of Polish academic, cultural, and artistic life and is one of Poland's most important economic hubs. It was the capital of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland from 1038 to 1569; the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth from 1569 to 1596, the Free City of Kraków from 1815 to 1846; the Grand Duchy of Cracow from 1846 to 1918; and Kraków Voivodeship from the 14th century to 1998. It has been the capital of Lesser Poland Voivodeship since 1999.
title: Kraków

text: In 1038, Kraków became the seat of the Polish government and subsequently evolved into a leading center of trade by the end of the 10th century. The city was characterized by the construction of brick buildings, including the Royal Wawel Castle and Romanesque churches such as St. Adalbert's, before being sacked and burned during the Mongol invasion of 1241. It was rebuilt in a practically identical manner based on a new location act, incorporating into the city by 1257 under the high duke Bolesław V the Chaste, who introduced a city rights model modeled on the Magdeburg law to grant tax benefits and trade privileges to citizens. The defensive walls were erected around the central section of Kazimierz in 1362, and a plot was set aside for the Augustinian order next to Skałka.
title: Kraków

It became a land-grant school in 1866, and its 933-acre main campus includes four National Historic Landmarks.
title: University of Wisconsin–Madison

text: The signing of the United States Declaration of Independence took place primarily on August 2, 1776, at Independence Hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. This historic event involved 56 delegates from the Second Continental Congress, who had previously endorsed the document approved on July 4, 1776. The text notes that the signers' names are grouped by state, with the exception of John Hancock, and that the states are arranged geographically from north to south.
title: Signing of the United States Declaration of Independence

text: The date of the signing of the Declaration of Independence remains a subject of historical debate, with most scholars agreeing that the document was finalized on August 2, 1776. This date, which occurred nearly a month after the Continental Congress approved the final draft on July 4, has long been considered the widely accepted truth rather than the popular belief that the document was signed on July 4.
title: Signing of the United States Declaration of Independence

text: In 2014, Nathan sublets Maxie Jones's apartment, and Detective West convinces Anna Devane to hire him so he can follow up his investigation into his sister's attempted murder. text: In C3 plants, the initial step of light-independent photosynthesis involves RuBisCO fixing carbon dioxide into 3-phosphoglycerate. However, because RuBisCO also acts as an oxygenase, some of the substrate is oxidized instead of carboxylated, leading to energy loss known as photorespiration. To circumvent this pathway, C4 plants utilize a specific leaf anatomy where chloroplasts reside in bundle sheath cells alongside mesophyll cells. Rather than direct fixation, CO2 is first incorporated into a 4-carbon organic acid within the chloroplasts. This specific acid then releases CO2 in the bundle sheath cells, where it is available to regenerate carbohydrates via the conventional C3 pathway.
title: C4 carbon fixation

This nerve serves as the primary connection between the nervous system and the skin of the leg, muscles of the posterior thigh, and the lower leg and foot. It is derived from spinal nerves L4 through S3 and contains fibers from both the anterior and posterior divisions of the lumbosacral plexus.
